description: Hey, we’re Team JARVIS! We’re tackling Flame in Freefall: building an AI dashboard that makes NASA’s fire-in-space research easy to explore, so astronauts heading to the Moon and Mars can stay safe. We’re into space, AI and building cool stuff, and still learning as we go.
summary: JARVIS is a web dashboard that shows how much of NASA’s microgravity fire research applies to the places astronauts will live next. Future Moon bases and pressurised rovers are expected to run at 30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less, and spacesuits at 100% oxygen, which makes materials far more flammable than in ISS cabin air. We turned 21 combustion investigations from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database into one structured, sourced dataset, then built tools to summarise, rank and interpret it for any crew habitat. The result is clear: almost every test was run in ordinary cabin air. Only 4 of 21 investigations reach Moon base conditions, none reach spacesuit conditions, and there is no partial-gravity data yet. JARVIS helps engineers and researchers see which results they can rely on and where new experiments are needed.
details:
What it does: the user picks a crew habitat (ISS, Moon base, pressurised rover, Mars base or spacesuit) and every part of the dashboard updates.

  • Explore: a mission briefing showing how many investigations tested oxygen and pressure that reach that habitat, plus real spacecraft fire incidents (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir, Artemis II) linked to related research.
  • Catalogue: every investigation with its fuel, oxygen, pressure, airflow, hardware, measurements, safety role (prevention, detection, suppression), findings and a link to its NASA source, with search, filters and a side-by-side comparison.
  • Gap map: the oxygen and pressure range each investigation tested, drawn against habitat zones. Empty space inside a zone is a research gap.
  • Rank: a transparent 0 to 100 relevance score per investigation for the chosen habitat, with adjustable weights and a breakdown of each score.
  • Simulator: set oxygen, pressure, airflow and gravity for a real tested material, see an illustrative flame-spread trend, and see which real investigations tested those conditions.
  • Ask JARVIS: questions in plain English, answered only from our dataset with a citation for every claim.

How it works: the dataset is a JSON file in which every value comes from a stated source (PSI records, NASA fact sheets, the 2015 Researcher’s Guide to ISS Combustion Science, published Saffire papers). Values a source does not state are left unknown and shown as unknown, never estimated. A validator script checks the data. For Ask JARVIS, the app selects the most relevant records, sends only those to a language model, and the server checks every citation in the answer against the records it sent, removing any that do not match. If the AI service is unavailable, the app still returns the matching records with their sources.

Benefits: it gives Artemis-era habitat designers, researchers and students one place to see what microgravity fire research covers and what it does not, and it supports choosing materials and planning the next experiments. The same evidence is relevant to fire safety in sealed spaces on Earth, such as mines, submarines and aircraft.

Tools: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, a Vercel serverless function, the Google Gemini API, GitHub, Node.js test and validation scripts.
